candidates.source_name: 1 Enoch (Ethiopian tradition) / Book of the Watchers (1 Enoch 1-36)
candidates.source_attribution: 1 Enoch 19:1, trans. R.H. Charles (1912). PD. Cf. 1 Cor 10:20.
candidates.draft_body:
1 Enoch (Ethiopian tradition) Book of the Watchers (1 Enoch 1-36) (c. 200 BC)

Uriel explains: 'Here shall stand the angels who have connected themselves with women, and their spirits assuming many different forms are defiling mankind and shall lead them astray into sacrificing to demons as gods' — the post-Flood human idolatry derived from demon-led seduction. Tewahedo reads this as the canonical-Jewish anchor for the New Testament's claim that pagan sacrifices are sacrifices 'to demons' (1 Cor 10:20: 'the things which the Gentiles sacrifice, they sacrifice to devils, and not to God'). The continuity between 1 Enoch's demonology and Paul's pagan-idolatry critique is one of the strongest inter-textual bridges the Tewahedo canon preserves.

candidates.source_attribution: 1 Enoch 19:3, trans. R.H. Charles (1912). PD.
candidates.draft_body:
1 Enoch (Ethiopian tradition) Book of the Watchers (1 Enoch 1-36) (c. 200 BC)

Enoch concludes his vision report: 'And I, Enoch, alone saw the vision, the ends of all things: and no man shall see as I have seen' — the Enochic claim to unique revelatory privilege. The 'no man shall see' establishes Enoch's prophetic singularity (until the eschaton's general revelation). Tewahedo reads this not as exclusivist boast but as commissioned-witness charter: Enoch sees so that he may report, his vision is recorded so that the elect may know what they could not otherwise know. The verse becomes the textual warrant for the Mäṣḥafä Hēnok's canonical-scriptural status: the unique vision requires preservation in inspired text.
